title: pH, pOH, and the Ion Product of Water

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part II, Class 11 — Equilibrium

summary: pH measures the acidity of a solution based on hydrogen ion concentration; pOH measures basicity based on hydroxide ion concentration; the two are linked because water's own ionization is constant at a given temperature (pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C).
explanation: Since pure water partially ionizes into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions with a constant product (Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C), the pH scale (0-14) provides a convenient way to express hydrogen ion concentration using a negative logarithm, which compresses the enormous range of possible concentrations into manageable numbers. A pH of 7 is neutral (equal H⁺ and OH⁻); below 7 is acidic (excess H⁺); above 7 is basic (excess OH⁻). Because pH is logarithmic, each whole-number change represents a TENFOLD change in hydrogen ion concentration.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a pH change of, say, 2 units represents a doubling of acidity — because the scale is logarithmic (base 10), a change of 2 units means a 100-fold change in [H⁺].
Assuming pH + pOH = 14 holds at any temperature — this relationship specifically depends on Kw = 10⁻¹⁴, which is only valid at 25°C; Kw changes with temperature.
examples: A solution with pH 3 has 10 times more H⁺ ions than a solution with pH 4.
genZNote: pH being logarithmic is the reason a 'small' pH drop from 7 to 5 is actually a 100x jump in acidity — the scale is deceptively compact.
